title.zh: 卷八十上 文苑列傳
title.raw: 卷八十上 文苑列傳 Volume 80a: Biographies of Writers 1

sentences.zh: 杜笃字季雅，京兆杜陵人也。

translations.literal: Du Du, courtesy name Jiya, was a native of Duling in Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du, whose courtesy name was Jiya, came from Duling in the metropolitan region of Jingzhao.

sentences.zh: 高祖延年，宣帝时为御史大夫。

translations.literal: His ancestor Yannian served as Imperial Counselor under Emperor Xuan of Han.
translations.idiomatic: An ancestor, Du Yannian, had served as Imperial Counselor during the reign of Emperor Xuan.

sentences.zh: 笃少博学，不修小节，不为乡人所礼。

translations.literal: In youth Du was broadly learned, kept no meticulous minor deportment, and was not treated with courtesy by his fellow villagers.
translations.idiomatic: As a young man Du Du read widely, scorned petty propriety, and won no respect from the people of his district.

sentences.zh: 居美阳，与美阳令游，数从请托，不谐，颇相恨。

translations.literal: He lived in Meiyang and kept company with the magistrate of Meiyang; repeatedly he asked favors through him; they did not succeed and came greatly to resent each other.
translations.idiomatic: While living in Meiyang he associated with the county magistrate and often tried to secure favors through him; when those efforts failed, the two grew mutually resentful.

translations.literal: The magistrate grew angry, arrested Du Du, and sent him to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: The magistrate, infuriated, had Du Du seized and escorted to the capital under arrest.

sentences.zh: 会大司马吴汉薨，光武诏诸儒诔之，笃于狱中为诔，辞最高，美帝之，赐帛免刑。

translations.literal: It happened that Grand Marshal Wu Han died; Guangwu ordered the scholars to compose dirges for him. Du Du, in prison, wrote a dirge; among them his text ranked highest; the emperor praised it and granted him silk, remitting punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Just then Grand Marshal Wu Han died, and Emperor Guangwu summoned the literati to mourn him in verse. From his cell Du Du submitted a dirge that surpassed the rest; the emperor admired it, rewarded him with silk, and released him without sentence.

sentences.zh: 笃以关中表里山河，先帝旧京，不宜改营洛邑，乃上奏《论都赋》曰：

translations.literal: Du held that within the passes mountains and rivers formed inner and outer ramparts, that it was the former capital of the late emperor, and that it was unsuitable to shift construction to Luoyang; thereupon he presented a memorial including his piece entitled Discourse on the Capital (Lun Du Fu), saying:
translations.idiomatic: Du Du argued that Guanzhong's ring of mountains and rivers and the old seat of the former emperor made it wrong to relocate the capital to Luoyang; he therefore submitted a memorial embedding his rhapsody Discourse on the Capital (Lun Du Fu), which begins:

sentences.zh: 臣闻知而复知，是为重知。

translations.literal: I have heard that to know and again to know is double knowing.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard it said that knowledge stacked upon knowledge is mere redundancy.

sentences.zh: 臣所欲言，陛下已知，故略其梗概，不敢具陈。

translations.literal: What Your servant wished to say Your Majesty already knows; therefore I outline only the rough sense and dare not set it forth completely.
translations.idiomatic: What I might say you already grasp, Sire, so I sketch only the gist and do not presume to rehearse every detail.

translations.literal: In antiquity Pan Geng cast off extravagance and practiced economy at Bo.
translations.idiomatic: Long ago Pan Geng forsook luxury and embraced austerity when he ruled from Bo.

translations.literal: When Cheng Zhou flourished, then they took up residence at central Luoyang.
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou reached their zenith when they established the royal seat at Luoyang in the central plain.

translations.literal: According to the times they determined the capital; they did not permanently fix one town.
translations.idiomatic: Each age chose its seat of government; no capital was meant to endure unchanged forever.

translations.literal: Among the deliberations of worthies and sages there was assuredly better and worse.
translations.idiomatic: Even among sage counsels some designs prove sounder than others.

translations.literal: In the bearing of hegemons and kings, clear insight stands utterly apart.
translations.idiomatic: The vision of a true king stands utterly apart from that of a mere hegemon.

translations.literal: In preserving the state, though the goal is one, the arts diverge.
translations.idiomatic: Guarding a realm aims at one end yet travels many roads.

translations.literal: Some abandon rugged barriers and strive for level ground.
translations.idiomatic: Some rulers forsake defensible heights for open terrain.

translations.literal: Some rely on mountains and rivers and swallow the Six States.
translations.idiomatic: Others hug mountains and rivers until they absorb every rival kingdom.

translations.literal: Some, grown wealthy and homesick, pay no heed to being struck from behind.
translations.idiomatic: Some, rich and longing for home, forget they may be attacked from the rear.

sentences.zh: 或掩空击虚，自蜀汉出，即日车驾，策由一卒；

translations.literal: Some strike empty places and void defenses, issuing from Hanzhong in a single day—the imperial carriage moves that day on one soldier's strategy.
translations.idiomatic: Some exploit an undefended gap, bursting out of Hanzhong so swiftly that the court rolls forward in a day on one strategist's plan.

translations.literal: Some understand yet refuse to follow; long they dwell on barren ridges.
translations.idiomatic: Some see the wiser course yet cling for years to bleak soil.

translations.literal: Your servant dares not presume to rely on any single argument.
translations.idiomatic: I would not presume to settle which approach is correct.

sentences.zh: 窃见司马相如、杨子云作辞赋以讽主上，臣诚慕之，伏作书一篇，名曰《论都》，谨并封奏如左。

translations.literal: Privately I observed Sima Xiangru and Yang Ziyun compose fu-rhapsodies to instruct their sovereign; Your servant sincerely admires them. Bowing low I have written one piece entitled On the Capital (Lun Du), respectfully I submit it sealed as follows.
translations.idiomatic: I recall how Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong crafted rhapsodies to counsel their rulers—examples I earnestly wish to emulate. Kneeling, I offer this essay titled On the Capital (Lun Du), sealed and laid before you as follows.

sentences.zh: 皇帝以建武十八年二月甲辰，升舆洛邑，巡于西岳。

translations.literal: On the jiachen day of the second month in the eighteenth Jianwu year, the emperor mounted his carriage at Luoyang and toured the western marchmount.
translations.idiomatic: In Jianwu 18, on the day jiachen of the second month, the Son of Heaven rode out from Luoyang to inspect the Western Marchmount.

sentences.zh: 推天时，顺斗极，排阊阖，入函谷，观厄于崤、黾，图险于陇、蜀。

translations.literal: He reckoned celestial timing, followed the Pole Star, pushed open Changhe Gate, entered Hangu Pass, surveyed the narrows at Xiao and Min, and mapped hazards in Long and Shu.
translations.idiomatic: He aligned the journey with Heaven's seasons, tracked the pole star through Changhe Gate into Hangu, studied the defiles of Xiao and Min, and traced the perilous terrain of Long and Shu.

translations.literal: In the third month on the day dingyou he arrived at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: That third month, on dingyou, he reached Chang'an.

sentences.zh: 经营宫室，伤愍旧京，即诏京兆，乃命扶风，斋肃致敬，告觐园陵。

translations.literal: He surveyed palace foundations, grieved for the old capital, issued edicts to Jingzhao and commanded Fufeng; fasting in purity he announced his visit to the imperial tombs.
translations.idiomatic: He toured the palace grounds, mourned the fallen glory of the former capital, ordered Jingzhao and Fufeng to prepare rites, and with solemn fasting announced his presence at the ancestral tombs.

sentences.zh: 凄然有怀祖之思，喟乎以思诸夏之隆。

translations.literal: Sadly he harbored thoughts of his ancestors; sighing, he recalled the splendor of the Hua domains.
translations.idiomatic: He was stirred by thoughts of his forebears and sighed over the grandeur the Central States once knew.

sentences.zh: 遂天旋云游，造舟于渭，北<方亢>泾流。

translations.literal: Thereupon Heaven seemed to wheel and clouds to drift; he built boats on the Wei and proceeded north along the current of the Jing.
translations.idiomatic: Then, as if heaven wheeled overhead, he launched vessels on the Wei and bent his course north along the Jing River.

sentences.zh: 千乘方毂，万骑骈罗，衍陈于岐、梁，东横乎大河。

translations.literal: A thousand chariots squared their hubs, ten thousand riders ranged in rows; formations stretched across Qi and Liang and bridged eastward over the great Yellow River.
translations.idiomatic: Thousands of chariots squared their tracks and myriad horsemen filled the roads; the columns swept Qi and Liang and stretched east across the Yellow River.

translations.literal: He buried offerings to Hou Tu and performed the suburban sacrifice at the suburban altar; the graph for Heaven is missing in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: He buried offerings to the Earth Spirit at the suburban altar and performed the suburban rites; the graph for Heaven is missing in the received text.

translations.literal: That same fourth month he returned to Luoyang, the eastern capital.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth month of that year he turned back toward Luoyang, the eastern capital.

sentences.zh: 明年，有诏复函谷关，作大驾宫、六王邸、高车厩于长安。

translations.literal: The next year an edict restored Hangu Pass and built the Grand Procession palace, the lodges for the six kings, and the tall-chariot stables at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: The following year an order reopened Hangu Pass and raised the Grand Procession Hall, guest residences for the royal princes, and tall-chariot stables at Chang'an.

sentences.zh: 修理东都城门，桥泾、渭，往往缮离观。

translations.literal: They repaired the gates of the eastern capital, bridged the Jing and Wei, and here and there restored detached watchtowers.
translations.idiomatic: Workers repaired the eastern capital's gates, spanned the Jing and Wei with bridges, and patched lookout towers along the way.

sentences.zh: 东临霸、浐，西望昆明，北登长平，规龙首，抚未央，覛平乐，仪建章。

translations.literal: Eastward they overlooked Ba and Chan; westward Kunming Pool; northward they climbed Changping, surveyed Longshou, paced Weiyang, viewed Pingle, and took the measure of Jianzhang.
translations.idiomatic: To the east lay Ba and Chan; to the west, Kunming Pool; climbing Changping in the north they traced Longshou Hill, walked Weiyang and Pingle, and measured Jianzhang Palace against the sky.

sentences.zh: 是时山东翕然狐疑，意圣朝之西都， 惧关门之反拒也。

translations.literal: At that time east of the mountains opinion wavered uneasily; people suspected the holy court's western capital and feared the passes might shut against them.
translations.idiomatic: People east of the mountains buzzed with doubt about the court's commitment to the western capital and dreaded that the frontier gates might slam shut.

sentences.zh: 客有为笃言：“彼□井之潢污，固不容夫吞舟；

translations.literal: A visitor said to Du: "That stagnant pond of a village well naturally cannot hold a ship that swallows great rivers;
translations.idiomatic: Someone urged Du Du: "That muddy pool by the village well cannot float a vessel built to swallow rivers;

sentences.zh: 且洛邑之渟瀯，曷足以居乎万乘哉？

translations.literal: Moreover how could Luoyang's sluggish pools suffice to house the carriage of the myriad riders?"
translations.idiomatic: moreover how could Luoyang's sluggish eddies sustain an emperor's train of ten thousand riders?"

sentences.zh: 咸阳守国利器，不可久虚，以示奸萌。

translations.literal: Xianyang is the keen weapon for guarding the state; it must not long stand empty lest treason sprout.
translations.idiomatic: Xianyang is the sharp edge with which the realm is defended; leave it vacant too long and rebellion stirs."

sentences.zh: ”笃未甚然其言也，故因为述大汉之崇，世据雍州之利，而今国家未暇之故，以喻客意。

translations.literal: Du was not wholly persuaded by these words; therefore he rehearsed the grandeur of the great Han, how generation after generation relied on Yongzhou's advantages and why the state today still lacked leisure—thus to instruct his visitor.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du did not quite accept this, so he laid out the Han dynasty's majesty, its long reliance on Yongzhou's strengths, and the pressing reasons the court still could not leave—meant to answer his visitor.

translations.literal: saying:
translations.idiomatic: He said:

sentences.zh: 昔在强秦，爰初开畔，霸自岐、雍，国富人衍，卒以并兼，桀虐作乱。

translations.literal: In the days of mighty Qin, when first they opened the frontiers, hegemony rose from Qi and Yong; the state grew rich and its people multiplied, until at last they annexed all—Jie-like cruelty bred rebellion.
translations.idiomatic: When all-powerful Qin first carved its realm, dominance sprang from Qi and Yong; wealth and population swelled until conquest unified the land—yet cruelty like Jie's invited revolt.

translations.literal: Heaven mandated a sage and entrusted the mandate to the great Han.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven ordained a sage-king and entrusted the mandate to great Han.

translations.literal: The great Han opened its foundation; the Supreme Founder earned merit.
translations.idiomatic: Han laid its foundations through the merit of the Supreme Founder.

sentences.zh: 斩白蛇，屯黑云，聚五星于东井，提干将而呵暴秦。

translations.literal: He slew the white serpent, massed black clouds, gathered the five planets above the Eastern Well, grasped the Ganjiang sword and shouted down brutal Qin.
translations.idiomatic: He cut the white serpent, drew black clouds about him, watched five planets gather over the Eastern Well, seized the storied sword Ganjiang, and roared down the cruelty of Qin.

sentences.zh: 蹈沧海，跨昆仑，奋彗光，扫项军，遂济人难，荡涤于泗、沂。

translations.literal: He trod the eastern seas, crossed Kunlun, brandished comet-like light, swept away Xiang Yu's host, rescued the people from calamity, and cleansed the Si and Yi rivers.
translations.idiomatic: He strode to the eastern sea, vaulted Kunlun, flashed like a comet across Xiang Yu's armies, lifted the people from disaster, and rinsed the Si and Yi clean of slaughter.

translations.literal: Liu Jing framed the plan; first they fixed the capital at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Jing shaped the strategy, and the capital was first settled at Chang'an.

translations.literal: The August Ancestor inherited that flow and guarded it through civil virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen inherited that tide of fortune and sustained it with humane government.

sentences.zh: 躬履节俭，侧身行仁，食不二味，衣无异采。

translations.literal: Personally he practiced thrift, humbled himself to enact benevolence, ate no second flavor at a meal, and wore no varied colors.
translations.idiomatic: He lived plainly, bent his person to kindness, took only one dish per meal, and wore undyed cloth without pattern.

sentences.zh: 赈人以农桑，率下以约已，曼丽之容不悦于目，郑、卫之声不过于耳，佞邪之臣不列于朝，巧伪之物不鬻于市，故能理升平而刑几措。

translations.literal: He relieved the people through farming and sericulture, led those below by restraining himself; lavish beauty did not please his eyes, the sounds of Zheng and Wei did not reach his ears, fawning ministers gained no place at court, crafty goods were not sold in the market—therefore he could achieve rising peace and nearly abolish punishments.
translations.idiomatic: He fed the people through tillage and silk, taught restraint by example; painted faces did not delight his eyes, the tunes of Zheng and Wei did not reach his ears, flatterers held no seat at court and shoddy wares no stall in the market—so peace ascended and punishments nearly vanished.

sentences.zh: 富衍于孝、景，功传于后嗣。

translations.literal: Wealth overflowed under Emperors Xiao and Jing; merit passed to later heirs.
translations.idiomatic: Prosperity spilled into the reigns of Xiaowen and Xiaojing; their achievement flowed to succeeding generations.

sentences.zh: 是时，孝武因其余财府帑之蓄，始有钩深图远之意，探冒顿之罪，校平城之仇。

translations.literal: At that time Emperor Wu, relying on surplus wealth stored in the treasury, first conceived intentions to probe deep and plan far, investigating Modun's crimes and measuring revenge for the Pingcheng defeat.
translations.idiomatic: Then Emperor Wu, drawing on overflowing treasuries, first dreamed of distant schemes—to reckon Modun's offenses and settle scores for the humiliation at Pingcheng.

sentences.zh: 遂命票骑，勤任卫青，勇惟鹰扬，军如流星，深之匈奴，割裂王庭，席卷漠北，叩勒祁连，横分单于，屠裂百蛮。

translations.literal: He therefore commissioned the Swift Cavalry general, heavily tasked Wei Qing; bravery soared like hawks, armies moved like meteors; he thrust deep into the Xiongnu, tore apart the royal court, swept the northern desert, stormed Qilian, split the Chanyu asunder, butchered the hundred barbarians.
translations.idiomatic: He charged the Swift Cavalry command and leaned hard on Wei Qing; armies swept like meteors and valor rose like hawks—deep into the steppe they shattered the royal court, rolled up the northern sands, stormed Qilian, split the Chanyu, and carved apart countless tribes.

sentences.zh: 烧罽帐，系阏氏，燔康居，灰珍奇，椎鸣镝，钉鹿蠡，驰坑岸，获昆弥，虏亻数侲，驱骡驴，御宛马，鞭□騠。

translations.literal: He burned felt tents, bound the Chanyu consort, set Kangju ablaze, reduced rare treasures to ash, smashed whistling arrows, pinned the Luoli prince, galloped ravines and cliffs, seized the Kunmi king, captured youthful hostages, drove mules and donkeys, mastered Ferghana horses, whipped swift coursers — the following graph is missing in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: They torched yurts, seized the Chanyu consort, burned Kangju to ash, shattered whistling arrows, pinned enemy princes, raced gorges and ridges, took the Wusun ruler and boy captives, drove pack animals and rode Ferghana steeds, laying the lash to every swift mount.

translations.literal: He expanded territory ten thousand li and awe shook the eight directions.
translations.idiomatic: Borders stretched ten thousand li and terror rang through every quarter.

translations.literal: He first established four frontier commanderies and held Dunhuang fast.
translations.idiomatic: They planted four western commanderies and anchored Dunhuang.

translations.literal: Border chiefdoms were folded in; one commandery governed an entire quarter.
translations.idiomatic: Dependent states along the frontier were folded in so that one commandery could oversee whole regions.

translations.literal: Marquises stood guard on the northern rim; Protectors of the Western Qiang were installed.
translations.idiomatic: Marquises anchored the northern marches; inspectors watched the western Qiang.

translations.literal: He drove the Di and Bo peoples and scattered wolves among Qiong and Zuo.
translations.idiomatic: They drove Di and Bo tribes and cleared wolf-like threats from Qiong and Zuo.

translations.literal: Eastward he rubbed against the Wuhuan and trampled the Huimo.
translations.idiomatic: To the east they brushed the Wuhuan and trampled the Huimo.

translations.literal: Southward he tethered Gouding and crossed swords with mighty Yue by water.
translations.idiomatic: To the south they leashed Gouding and crossed blades with powerful Yue along the rivers.

translations.literal: He mutilated the tattooed tribesmen; seas foamed with blood.
translations.idiomatic: They broke the tattooed southern peoples until the seas foamed crimson.

translations.literal: Commanderies reached Rinan; banners streamed toward Zhuya.
translations.idiomatic: Counties stretched to Rinan and standards fluttered toward Zhuya.

translations.literal: A colonel watched the southeast and Huangzhi was swept in as well.
translations.idiomatic: A southern colonel held the southeast until even Huangzhi fell within reach.

sentences.zh: 连缓耳，琐雕题，摧天督，牵象犀，椎蚌蛤，碎琉璃，甲玳瑁，戕觜觿。

translations.literal: Linked ear-loops and carved foreheads; Tian-du destroyed; elephants and rhinos dragged home; shells smashed; glass shattered; tortoise shell and hawksbill crushed; pipes and jades broken.
translations.idiomatic: Long-ear tribes and tattooed foreheads were yanked into submission—armies shattered Tian-du, hauled back elephants and rhinos, crushed shells and glass, smashed tortoise and horn ornaments.

sentences.zh: 于是同穴裘褐之域，共川鼻饮之国，莫不袒跣稽颡，失气虏伏。

translations.literal: Thus in lands where cave-dwellers wore furs and peoples drank from the same rivers with their noses, none failed to bare feet, knock foreheads to earth, lose their breath, and crouch like captured beasts.
translations.idiomatic: Even peoples who dwelt in caves and furs and drank river-water through their noses came barefoot to knock their heads in the dust, breathless and prostrate.

sentences.zh: 非夫大汉之世盛，世借雍土之饶，得御外理内之术，孰能致功若斯！

translations.literal: Were it not for the Han's glorious age, borrowing Yongzhou's bounty and wielding arts to manage within and without, who could have wrought merit like this!
translations.idiomatic: Without Han's golden age, Yongzhou's abundance, and skill at ruling interior and frontier alike, who could have piled up such deeds!

sentences.zh: 故创业于高祖，嗣传于孝惠，德隆于太宗，财衍于孝景，威盛于圣武，政行于宣、元，侈极于成、哀、祚缺于孝平。

translations.literal: Thus the enterprise began with the Supreme Founder, passed to Emperor Xiaohui, virtue peaked with Emperor Wen, wealth accumulated under Emperor Jing, might crested with Emperor Wu, policy flourished under Emperors Xuan and Yuan, extravagance peaked under Emperors Cheng and Ai, and the mandate cracked under Emperor Xiaoping.
translations.idiomatic: The line began with Gaozu, flowed through Emperor Hui, rose in virtue with Emperor Wen, spread wealth with Emperor Jing, blazed in might with Emperor Wu, ran smoothly under Emperors Xuan and Yuan, burned brightest in excess under Cheng and Ai, and shattered under young Emperor Ping.

sentences.zh: 传世十一，历载三百，德衰而复盈，道微而复章，皆莫能迁于雍州，而背于咸阳。

translations.literal: Eleven generations passed across three hundred years; virtue waned then waxed again, the Way dimmed then brightened—yet none could shift the seat from Yongzhou or turn their back on Xianyang.
translations.idiomatic: Eleven reigns spanned three centuries—power ebbed and flowed, the Way dimmed and returned—yet no ruler could drag the capital from Yongzhou or turn away from Xianyang.

sentences.zh: 宫室寝庙，山陵相望，高显弘丽，可思可荣，羲、农已来，无兹著明。

translations.literal: Palace halls and ancestral shrines, imperial tumuli facing one another—lofty, splendid, stirring and glorious—since Fu Xi and Shen Nong none has shone so bright.
translations.idiomatic: Palaces and tombs crowd the horizon, vast and splendid, stirring pride—nothing since Fu Xi and Shen Nong has gleamed so visibly.

sentences.zh: 夫雍州本帝皇所以育业、霸王所以衍功，战士角难之场也。

translations.literal: Now Yongzhou is the ground where emperors nurture enterprise and hegemons enlarge merit; it is the arena where warriors contend with hardship.
translations.idiomatic: Yongzhou is where emperors cultivate destiny and hegemons magnify achievement—the crucible where soldiers wrestle fate.

translations.literal: What the "Tribute of Yu" records ranks its fields as the highest grade.
translations.idiomatic: The "Tribute of Yu" ranks its soil at the top of the scale.

translations.literal: A thousand li of fertile plain; marshes and moors stretch to the horizon.
translations.idiomatic: Rich fields extend a thousand li; wetlands roll away on every side.

translations.literal: It reliably grows the five grains; mulberry and hemp flourish in orderly rows.
translations.idiomatic: The five grains grow in abundance; mulberry and hemp thrive in neat rows.

sentences.zh: 滨据南山，带以泾、渭，号曰陆海，蠢生万类。

translations.literal: It borders the Southern Mountains and is girded by the Jing and Wei; called the "land within the seas," it teems with every kind of life.
translations.idiomatic: Braced against the Southern Mountains and belted by Jing and Wei, it is styled the inland sea where countless creatures thrive.

translations.literal: Catalpa, nanmu, sandalwood, and mulberry bear fruit in season.
translations.idiomatic: Catalpa, citrus, sandalwood, and mulberry yield fruit in due season.

sentences.zh: 畎渎润淤，水泉灌溉，渐泽成川，粳稻陶遂。

translations.literal: Irrigation channels flush silt; springs water the fields; moisture spreads until rivers form and rice ripens everywhere.
translations.idiomatic: Sluices scour silt while springs feed the plots; moisture spreads into branching streams until rice ripens far and wide.

translations.literal: The soil is so rich that an acre costs a pound of gold.
translations.idiomatic: The earth is so fertile that land sells for a pound of gold the acre.

translations.literal: Fields stretch ridge upon ridge; hoes and mattocks work the woods.
translations.idiomatic: Farmland rolls without end; farmers hoe among the groves.

translations.literal: Slash-and-burn and drifting seed bring shallow labor yet deep yield.
translations.idiomatic: Fire-clearing and scattered sowing ask little labor yet yield richly.

sentences.zh: 既有蓄积，厄塞四临：四被陇、蜀，南通汉中，北据谷口，东阻嵚岩。

translations.literal: Once stores are piled high, barriers close it on four sides: Long and Shu to the west, Hanzhong to the south, Gukou to the north, precipitous heights to the east.
translations.idiomatic: With granaries full, four ramparts hem it in—Long and Shu on the west, Hanzhong on the south, Gukou on the north, sheer cliffs on the east.

translations.literal: Hangu Pass guards the heights; roads from east of the mountains end here.
translations.idiomatic: Hangu's steep barrier chokes the road; eastern approaches dead-end here.

translations.literal: Lines arrayed along Qian and Long choke off the western Rong.
translations.idiomatic: Camps along the Qian and Long valleys bottle up the western Rong.

translations.literal: Holding Bao and Xie bars the lands south of the ridge.
translations.idiomatic: Guarding Bao and Xie seals the country south of the divide.

translations.literal: Closing the mouths and cutting the fords—the northern regions find no approach.
translations.idiomatic: Seal the passes and cut the ferries and the northern marches have no easy crossing.

translations.literal: The currents of the Hong and Wei flow straight into the Yellow River.
translations.idiomatic: The Hong and Wei rivers run straight into the Yellow River.

translations.literal: Ten thousand great ships ferry grain one after another.
translations.idiomatic: Ten thousand barges shuttle grain in endless trains.

translations.literal: Eastward they bind the blue sea; westward they net the drifting sands.
translations.idiomatic: To the east lies the sea's harness; to the west the drifting sands are gathered in.

translations.literal: North and south share one resonance; the Central States dwell in harmony.
translations.idiomatic: From north to south a single rule holds; the Hua lands rest at peace.

translations.literal: City walls rise a hundred chi; passes guard every choke point.
translations.idiomatic: Walls soar a hundred feet; fortresses choke every vital gap.

translations.literal: Many passes and bridges clasp the terrain like belts.
translations.idiomatic: Ravines and bridges pinch the roads like belt-straps.

translations.literal: One soldier works the thunder-engine and a thousand men are stalled.
translations.idiomatic: Raise one traction trebuchet and a thousand attackers stall.

translations.literal: One man brandishes a halberd and three armies collapse.
translations.idiomatic: A single warrior swinging a ji can rout three armies.

sentences.zh: 地势便利，介胄剽悍，可与守近，利以攻远。

translations.literal: Advantageous terrain, hardened armor—good for defending what is near, profitable for striking far.
translations.idiomatic: The ground favors defense at hand and offense at a distance; mail and helm breed fierceness.

translations.literal: Soldiers find protection easily; men need not strip for desperate combat.
translations.idiomatic: Troops win shelter readily; men fight fully armed instead of baring their breasts in despair.

translations.literal: Twelve regions in all—this is the fat of the land.
translations.idiomatic: Twelve provinces in sum—this is the empire's larder.

sentences.zh: 用霸则兼并，先据则功殊；

translations.literal: Employ hegemony and you annex; seize the initiative first and merit differs.
translations.idiomatic: Use brute strength and you swallow rivals; seize the advantage early and your achievement stands apart.

sentences.zh: 修文则财衍，行武则士要；

translations.literal: Cultivate letters and wealth overflows; wield arms and warriors answer like a tightened cord.
translations.idiomatic: Pursue culture and treasure accumulates; wield arms and soldiers answer like a drawn cord.

sentences.zh: 为政则化上，篡逆则难诛；

translations.literal: When governance is upright transformation lifts upward; when usurpation occurs, traitors are hard to extirpate.
translations.idiomatic: Good government lifts custom upward; once usurpation appears, rebels prove hard to root out.

sentences.zh: 进攻则百克，退守则有余：斯固帝王之渊囿，而守国之利器也。

translations.literal: Attack and every assault succeeds; withdraw and defense holds surplus: thus it is indeed the imperial breeding-ground and the state's sharp blade.
translations.idiomatic: Strike outward and victory follows; draw inward and reserves remain—this is the emperor's park and the nation's sword.

sentences.zh: 逮及亡新，时汉之衰，偷忍渊囿，篡器慢违，徒以势便，莫能卒危。

translations.literal: When it came to doomed Xin, at the hour of Han's decline, sneaking patience in the imperial preserve, usurping the vessels and slighting the mandate, relying merely on convenience—they could not in the end bring down the peril.
translations.idiomatic: When Xin fell and Han tottered, Wang Mang lurked in that same fertile basin, stole the regalia and mocked Heaven's charge, trusting only convenience—yet even he could not finish the ruin he began.

translations.literal: After eighteen years of usurpation, punishment came from the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Eighteen years into his reign, retribution arrived out of the capital.

translations.literal: Heaven invested Gengshi but could not hold the reins.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven raised up Emperor Gengshi, yet no hand could steady the traces.

translations.literal: Careless hoarding invited bandits and once again brought the Red Eyebrows.
translations.idiomatic: Slipshod guarding drew marauders and summoned the Red Eyebrows anew.

translations.literal: Within the seas storm-clouds boiled; the Hua heartland flickered toward extinction.
translations.idiomatic: The empire seethed like storm clouds; the Central States verged on collapse.

translations.literal: Many dragons battled together; none could tell right from wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Contenders rose like rival dragons; no one knew which cause was just.

sentences.zh: 于时圣帝，赫然申威，荷天人之符，兼不世之姿。

translations.literal: Then the sage emperor blazed forth his majesty, bore the tally uniting Heaven and man, and united an aura not seen in ordinary ages.
translations.idiomatic: Then our sage lord revealed awe-inspiring might, shouldered the mandate of Heaven and humanity, and embodied a presence beyond common kings.

sentences.zh: 受命于皇上，获助于灵祇。

translations.literal: He received the charge from High Heaven and aid from the numinous spirits.
translations.idiomatic: He took his mandate from on high and won help from the spirits.

translations.literal: He raised his title at Gaoyi and seized banners on every quarter.
translations.idiomatic: He proclaimed his reign from Gaoyi and planted standards on every front.

translations.literal: Ministers who first devised strategy plotted surprises beyond reckoning;
translations.idiomatic: The counselors who framed the opening moves devised stratagems no one foresaw;

translations.literal: troops roaring with rage;
translations.idiomatic: Behind them came armies that howled with rage;

translations.literal: like tigers and hornless dragons.
translations.idiomatic: fierce as tigers and hornless dragons.

translations.literal: Wherever the army turned, nothing escaped being swept flat.
translations.idiomatic: Wherever those hosts marched, nothing stood uncut.

sentences.zh: 盖夫燔鱼剸蛇，莫之方斯。

translations.literal: Surely even burning fish and slicing snakes cannot match this.
translations.idiomatic: Not even the oldest tales of burning fish and slicing serpents equal such speed.

translations.literal: A great shout east of the mountains shook the drifting sands.
translations.idiomatic: Their war cry east of the mountains rattled the sands beyond the frontier.

sentences.zh: 要龙渊，首镆铘，命腾太白，亲发狼、弧。

translations.literal: He girded the sword of Longyuan, brandished Moyé, commanded the star Tai-bai to sweep aloft, and himself drew the Bow and Wolf constellations.
translations.idiomatic: He belted Longyuan, raised Moyé, called on the White Planet to rise, and shot on foot toward Bow and Wolf.

sentences.zh: 南禽公孙，北背强胡，西平陇、冀，东据洛都。

translations.literal: Southward he caged Gongsun Shu; northward he turned back the fierce Hu; westward he pacified Long and Ji; eastward he seized the Luoyang capital.
translations.idiomatic: To the south he trapped Gongsun Shu; to the north he threw back the steppe riders; to the west he quieted Long and Ji; to the east he anchored the seat at Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 乃廓平帝宇，济蒸人于涂炭，成兆庶之□，遂兴复乎大汉。

translations.literal: Thus he cleared the imperial realm, lifted the people from fire and flood, secured the teeming millions' welfare where one graph is missing in the received text, and revived great Han.
translations.idiomatic: He swept the world clear, snatched the common folk from ruin, secured the multitude's well-being—one graph missing here—and thus restored the Han house.

sentences.zh: 今天下新定，矢石之勤始瘳，而主上方以边垂为忧，忿葭萌之不柔，未遑于论都而遗思雍州也。

translations.literal: Now the realm is newly settled; the wounds of arrow and stone have barely scarred, yet our ruler already frets the frontiers, burns over Jiameng's defiance, and has no leisure to debate capitals while forgetting Yongzhou.
translations.idiomatic: The empire is only just stable; the scars of siege are still fresh, yet the throne worries about the marches, bristles at stubborn Jiameng, and cannot spare breath for capital polemics while Yongzhou slips from mind.

sentences.zh: 方躬劳圣思，以率海内，厉抚名将，略地疆外，信威于征伐，展武乎荒裔。

translations.literal: Just now he bends his own sagely thought to lead the interior, heartens famous generals, extends control beyond the borders, spreads awe through campaigns, and displays arms in the farthest wilds.
translations.idiomatic: He pours his own counsel into governing the heartland, steadies renowned commanders, pushes the frontier outward, lets punitive awe speak for itself, and flaunts force even in the outer wastes.

sentences.zh: 若夫文身鼻饮缓耳之主，椎结左衽□鍝之君，东南殊俗不羁之国，西北绝域难制之邻，靡不重译纳贡，请为籓臣。

translations.literal: As for lords who tattoo their bodies, drink through the nose, or lengthen their ears, chiefs with topknots and left-lapped robes with belt ornaments damaged in the text, exotic realms of the southeast that defy control, remote neighbors of the northwest hard to bind—none failed to send relay interpreters with tribute and beg to become vassals.
translations.idiomatic: From tattooed chiefs with bored ears to skirted lords in far provinces—one character is damaged here—southeastern peoples outside the norm and northwestern neighbors beyond easy rule: every one sent interpreters, delivered tribute, and asked to serve as outer subjects.

translations.literal: The sovereign still demurs and will not boast of military toil.
translations.idiomatic: The Son of Heaven stays modest and refuses to trumpet battlefield glory.

sentences.zh: 意以为获无用之虏，不如安有益之民；

translations.literal: His meaning is that useless captives are a poor exchange for settled, productive people;
translations.idiomatic: He judges worthless prisoners a bad bargain beside citizens who can feed the realm;

sentences.zh: 略荒裔之地，不如保殖五谷之渊；

translations.literal: seizing barren border wastes is a poor exchange for guarding the granaries of the five grains;
translations.idiomatic: grabbing sterile frontier acres matters less than tending the breadbasket heartland;

sentences.zh: 远救于已亡，不若近而存存也。

translations.literal: distant succor for what is already lost cannot compare with cherishing what still lives nearby.
translations.idiomatic: rescuing the ruined far away cannot match protecting what still breathes close at hand.

sentences.zh: 今国家躬修道德，吐惠含仁，湛恩沾洽，时风显宣。

translations.literal: Today the court cultivates virtue in person, exhales kindness and breathes benevolence; deep grace saturates the land and timely instruction shines abroad.
translations.idiomatic: The state walks the moral path openly, seasons policy with mercy, lets generous edicts soak every district, and lets honest winds blow everywhere.

sentences.zh: 徒垂意于持平守实，务在爱育元元，苟有便于王政者，圣主纳焉。

translations.literal: It aims only at balance and substance, cherishing the common people; whatever serves royal government, the sage ruler adopts.
translations.idiomatic: Its aim is steady fairness and tangible good for the black-haired masses; any measure that truly helps the throne, the sage accepts.

translations.literal: Why?
translations.idiomatic: Why so?

sentences.zh: 物罔挹而不损，道无隆而不移，阳盛则运，阴满则亏，故存不忘亡，安不讳危，虽有仁义，犹设城池也。

translations.literal: Nothing can be poured out without diminishing; no Way waxes without shifting; when yang peaks it moves on; when yin fills it ebbs—therefore even while preserving life remember ruin, and even in safety speak of peril; though benevolence and right prevail, still build walls and moats.
translations.idiomatic: Pour from any vessel and it empties; lift any doctrine and it shifts; thriving yang rolls onward, filling yin withdraws—so remember doom in days of peace and name danger in times of calm; even under humane rule, ramparts remain necessary.

sentences.zh: 客以利器不可久虚，而国家亦不忘乎西都，何必去洛邑之渟瀯与？

translations.literal: The visitor argues that keen weapons cannot stand idle long, and the court has not forgotten the western capital—why then abandon Luoyang's sheltered pools?
translations.idiomatic: Your guest says the realm's sword cannot hang unused and the west still matters—must we therefore quit Luoyang's sheltered basin?

translations.literal: Later Du Du served as Literary Instructor in his commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du later held the post of commandery Literary Instructor.

sentences.zh: 以目疾，二十余年不窥京师。

translations.literal: Because of an eye ailment he did not visit the capital for more than twenty years.
translations.idiomatic: Eye trouble kept him away from the capital for over two decades.

sentences.zh: 笃之外高祖破羌将军辛武贤，以武略称。

translations.literal: Du's maternal great-grandfather was General Who Subdues the Qiang, Xin Wu-xian, famed for martial strategy.
translations.idiomatic: On his mother's side his great-grandfather was Xin Wu-xian, General Who Subdues the Qiang, celebrated for strategic daring.

sentences.zh: 笃常叹曰：“杜氏文明善政，而笃不任为吏；

translations.literal: Du often sighed: "The Du house shines in civil governance, yet Du cannot bear office;
translations.idiomatic: Du Du would sigh: "My clan excels at humane rule, yet I am no magistrate;

sentences.zh: 辛氏秉义经武，而笃又怯于事。

translations.literal: the Xin clan upholds righteousness and arms itself with the classics, yet Du is timid in practical affairs.
translations.idiomatic: the Xin clan pairs integrity with martial readiness, yet I shrink from responsibility.

translations.literal: Five generations within and without—by Du's generation the vigor has faded!"
translations.idiomatic: Five generations on—by my time the spark has guttered out!"

translations.literal: His younger sister married into the Ma clan of Fufeng.
translations.idiomatic: A younger sister wed into the Ma family of Fufeng.

sentences.zh: 建初三年，车骑将军马防击西羌，请笃为从事中郎，战没于射姑山。

translations.literal: In the third Jianchu year, General of Chariots and Cavalry Ma Fang campaigned against the western Qiang and invited Du Du as senior attendant; Du Du fell in battle at Mount Shegu.
translations.idiomatic: In Jianchu 3 Ma Fang, General of Chariots and Cavalry, struck the western Qiang and named Du Du senior attendant; Du Du died fighting at Shegu Mountain.

sentences.zh: 所著赋、诔、吊、书、赞、《七言》、《女诫》及杂文，凡十八篇。

translations.literal: His writings include fu, dirges, condolences, letters, encomia, 《Seven-Character Lines》, 《Admonitions for Women》, and miscellaneous pieces—eighteen works in all.
translations.idiomatic: He left fu, laments, memorial essays, letters, praises, 《Seven-Character Lines》, 《Admonitions for Women》, and assorted prose—eighteen titles altogether.

translations.literal: He also composed fifteen chapters of 《Discourse on the Manifest Age》.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote fifteen chapters more under the title 《Discourse on the Manifest Age》.

translations.literal: His son Shuo was a daring knight celebrated for trade and wealth.
translations.idiomatic: His son Shuo lived boldly and made a name in commerce.

sentences.zh: 王隆字文山，冯翊云阳人也。

translations.literal: Wang Long, courtesy name Wenshan, was a native of Yunyang in Pingyi.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Long, called Wenshan, hailed from Yunyang in Pingyi commandery.

sentences.zh: 王莽时，以父任为郎，后避难河西，为窦融左护军。

translations.literal: Under Wang Mang he entered the corps of gentlemen through his father's privilege; later he fled to Hexi and became Dou Rong's Protector General of the Left.
translations.idiomatic: In Wang Mang's day he became a gentleman cadet by hereditary privilege; when turmoil rose he escaped to Hexi and served Dou Rong as left protector general.

translations.literal: During the Jianwu era he was magistrate of Xinji.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Guangwu he governed Xinji county.

sentences.zh: 能文章，所著诗、赋、铭、书凡二十六篇。

translations.literal: Skilled at composition, he wrote poems, fu, inscriptions, and letters—twenty-six pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: He excelled at letters and left poems, fu, inscriptions, and essays—twenty-six pieces.

sentences.zh: 初，王莽末，沛国史岑子孝亦以文章显，莽以为谒者，著颂、诔、《复神》、《说疾》凡四篇。

translations.literal: Earlier, at the end of Wang Mang's reign, Shi Cen of Pei, styled Zixiao, also rose to fame through writing; Mang appointed him usher, and he composed encomia, dirges, 《Return of the Spirits》, and 《On Illness》—four works.
translations.idiomatic: Near Wang Mang's fall, Shi Cen of Pei—style Zixiao—won notice as a writer; Mang named him court usher, and he produced hymns, laments, 《Return of the Spirits》, and 《On Illness》—four compositions.

sentences.zh: 夏恭字敬公，梁国蒙人也。

translations.literal: Xia Gong, courtesy name Jinggong, was a native of Meng in the Liang kingdom.
translations.idiomatic: Xia Gong, known as Jinggong, came from Meng in Liang.

sentences.zh: 习《韩诗》、《孟氏易》，讲授门徒常千余人。

translations.literal: He studied 《Han Shi Poetry》 and 《Meng Lineage Changes》; his lecture hall often held more than a thousand disciples.
translations.idiomatic: He mastered the 《Han Shi Poetry》 tradition and the 《Meng Lineage Changes》 school and routinely taught over a thousand students.

sentences.zh: 王莽末，盗贼从横，攻没郡县。

translations.literal: At the end of Wang Mang's reign bandits ran rampant and overran counties.
translations.idiomatic: When Wang Mang collapsed, bandits swarmed and seized county seats.

sentences.zh: 恭以恩信为众所附，拥兵固守，独安全。

translations.literal: Gong won the people's attachment through kindness and good faith; he held his troops fast and alone remained secure.
translations.idiomatic: Xia Gong earned loyalty through humane dealing; he kept his men steady and alone preserved his district.

sentences.zh: 光武即位，嘉其忠果，召拜郎中，再迁太山都尉。

translations.literal: When Guangwu took the throne he praised Gong's loyalty and resolve, summoned him as gentleman, and twice promoted him to commandant of Taishan.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Guangwu admired his steadfast courage, called him to court as a gentleman, and twice raised him to Taishan commandant.

translations.literal: He reconciled and gathered the common people and deeply won their affection.
translations.idiomatic: He soothed the populace and truly earned their hearts.

sentences.zh: 恭善为文，著赋、颂、诗、《励学》凡二十篇。

translations.literal: Gong excelled at letters and composed fu, hymns, poems, and 《Encourage Study》—twenty pieces.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote fu, songs, verse, and 《Encourage Study》—twenty works.

sentences.zh: 年四十九卒官，诸儒共谥曰宣明君。

translations.literal: He died in office at forty-nine; Ru scholars jointly styled him Lord Illustrious Bright.
translations.idiomatic: He died on duty at forty-nine; Confucian scholars honored him posthumously as Lord Illustrious Bright.

sentences.zh: 子牙，少习家业，著赋、颂、赞、诔凡四十篇。

translations.literal: His son Ziya studied the family curriculum in youth and composed fu, hymns, praises, and dirges—forty pieces.
translations.idiomatic: His son Ziya trained at home and left forty fu, songs, eulogies, and laments.

sentences.zh: 举孝廉，早卒，乡人号曰文德先生。

translations.literal: Recommended as filial and incorrupt, he died young; villagers styled him Master Literary Virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Recommended as filial and honest, he died young; locals dubbed him Master Literary Virtue.

sentences.zh: 傅毅字武仲，扶风茂陵人也。

translations.literal: Fu Yi, courtesy name Wuzhong, was a native of Maoling in Fufeng.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi, called Wuzhong, came from Maoling in Fufeng.

translations.literal: In youth he studied broadly.
translations.idiomatic: As a boy he read widely.

sentences.zh: 永平中，于平陵习章句，因作《迪志诗》曰：

translations.literal: During Yongping he practiced textual analysis at Pingling and thereupon composed 《Poem Expressing Resolve》, saying:
translations.idiomatic: In the Yongping era he parsed classics at Pingling and drafted his 《Poem Expressing Resolve》, which opens:

translations.literal: Ah, you throng of gentlemen—seize this hour and strive.
translations.idiomatic: Hear me, all you scholars—use this moment and press onward.

translations.literal: Sun and moon race onward—can you say they ever wheel back!
translations.idiomatic: The sun and moon never pause—who would claim they ever return!

translations.literal: Pity my striving—my strength cannot reach the goal.
translations.idiomatic: I pity these labors—my sinews fail the task.

translations.literal: In this feeble calamity I have nowhere to plant lasting roots.
translations.idiomatic: Beset by weakness I find nowhere to raise a lasting stand.

translations.literal: Ah, glorious our ancestor, shining in the Yin realm.
translations.idiomatic: Great our forebear, famed throughout Yin.

translations.literal: Twofold like Yi Yin—able to brighten his norm.
translations.idiomatic: Twin pillars like Yi Yin—shining through his standard.

translations.literal: Wuding revived Shang; ministers of the Yi clan stood as royal pillars.
translations.idiomatic: King Wuding lifted Shang anew; Yi lineage ministers became the royal limbs.

translations.literal: Thus they became thighs and arms; myriad regions took their measure from them.
translations.idiomatic: They served as arms and legs; every state fell under their rule.

translations.literal: Generation on generation bore virtue down to my eminent father.
translations.idiomatic: Virtue flowed generation after generation until my honored father.

translations.literal: Secure and gracious, he continued and cultivated that Way.
translations.idiomatic: He guarded gentle excellence and walked that path onward.

sentences.zh: 汉之中叶，俊乂式序，秩彼殷宗，光此勋绪。

translations.literal: Mid-Han ranked worthy talent; good order matched the Yin house and brightened this merit-thread.
translations.idiomatic: At Han's midpoint talents stood ranked like the Yin kings; order echoed their house and lit our lineage.

translations.literal: I, this little child, am coarse and cannot attain them.
translations.idiomatic: I am but a weakling, too base to match them.

translations.literal: I fear our generations' fierce virtue may fall away from here.
translations.idiomatic: I dread our ancestral fire guttering out at my feet.

translations.literal: Who can scour the turbid and rinse me clean?
translations.idiomatic: Who will scour this murk and wash me pure?

translations.literal: Who can illumine the dark and open my childish blindness?
translations.idiomatic: Who will light this gloom and wake my boyish ignorance?

translations.literal: The ancestors left lessons—I question them and take instruction.
translations.idiomatic: Forebears left counsel—I probe it and accept their charge.

translations.literal: They instruct my worthy tasks and teach my broad learning.
translations.idiomatic: They chart noble work and urge wide study.

translations.literal: Thus I join friends to trace these ancient norms.
translations.idiomatic: So I band with friends to recover old standards.

translations.literal: Partings and unions through mornings and nights—may I never slack or stray.
translations.idiomatic: Night and day in earnest union—may I never slack or stumble.

translations.literal: Orderly are the great plans; patterns guide every model.
translations.idiomatic: Grand designs lie ordered; norms bind every pattern.

translations.literal: Without diligence there is no clarity; without unity no depth.
translations.idiomatic: Without zeal nothing shines; without singleness nothing sounds.

sentences.zh: 农夫不怠，越有黍稷，谁能云作，考之居息？

translations.literal: If farmers never slack, millet and sorghum abound—who claims harvest comes without labor at home?
translations.idiomatic: Farmers who never idle reap grain and beans—who says harvest needs no effort at the hearth?

translations.literal: Two pursuits ruin the task and often drain my strength.
translations.idiomatic: Two aims wreck the work and sap my strength.

translations.literal: Like broad highways they lead nowhere final.
translations.idiomatic: Like open highways they never reach a bound.

translations.literal: Two aims unfulfilled—thus my heart wearies.
translations.idiomatic: Both goals unmet—so my heart tires.

translations.literal: Like listening to many voices at once—confusion of sound.
translations.idiomatic: Like hearing every side at once—only noise remains.

translations.literal: Alas, gentlemen—never indulge yourselves.
translations.idiomatic: Alas, good men—never sink into ease.

translations.literal: Departing years flow like water; leisure is scarce.
translations.idiomatic: Years stream away; rest is rare.

translations.literal: Marching halts again and again—how reach the end.
translations.idiomatic: The journey halts repeatedly—how can one ever finish.

translations.literal: Diligent morning and night—thus match beginning and end.
translations.idiomatic: Work dawn to dusk—then beginning matches the close.

sentences.zh: 毅以显宗求贤不笃，士多隐处，故作《七激》以为讽。

translations.literal: Yi believed Emperor Ming did not seek worthies earnestly enough and many scholars hid away; therefore he composed 《Seven Exhortations》 as remonstrance.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi felt Emperor Ming courted talent too timidly and scholars stayed hidden, so he wrote 《Seven Exhortations》 to needle the throne.

sentences.zh: 建初中，肃宗博召文学之士，以毅为兰台令史，拜郎中，与班固、贾逵共典校书。

translations.literal: In mid-Jianchu Emperor Zhang broadly summoned literary men: he appointed Yi Orchid Terrace clerk, promoted him to gentleman, and had him collate texts with Ban Gu and Jia Kui.
translations.idiomatic: Midway through Jianchu, Emperor Zhang called literati widely—named Fu Yi to the Orchid Terrace, made him a gentleman, and paired him with Ban Gu and Jia Kui to collate the canon.

sentences.zh: 毅追美李明皇帝功德最盛，而庙颂未立，乃依《清庙》作《显宗颂》十篇奏之，由是文雅显于朝廷。

translations.literal: Yi praised Emperor Ming's virtue and merit as supreme, yet no temple hymn stood; accordingly he modeled 《Qing Temple Ode》 and presented ten chapters of 《Hymns for Emperor Ming》, after which his prose graced the court.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi argued that Emperor Ming's deeds topped every predecessor yet lacked a temple hymn, so he echoed 《Qing Temple Ode》 in ten 《Hymns for Emperor Ming》; afterward his style dominated court letters.

sentences.zh: 车骑将军马防，外戚尊重，请毅为军司马，待以师友之礼。

translations.literal: General of Chariots and Cavalry Ma Fang, honored as an in-law, invited Yi as army major and treated him with teacher-and-friend courtesy.
translations.idiomatic: Ma Fang, General of Chariots and Cavalry and favored kinsman, took Fu Yi as army chief of staff and honored him like a mentor.

translations.literal: When the Ma clan fell he was dismissed and returned home.
translations.idiomatic: When the Ma fell from power he lost office and went home.

sentences.zh: 永元元年，车骑将军窦宪，复请毅为主记室，崔骃为主簿。

translations.literal: In the first Yongyuan year Grand General Dou Xian again named Yi chief secretary and Cui Yin registrar.
translations.idiomatic: Yongyuan 1 saw Dou Xian, Grand General, recall Fu Yi as chief clerk and name Cui Yin registrar.

sentences.zh: 及宪迁大将军，复以毅为司马，班固为中护军。

translations.literal: When Dou was promoted Grand General, Yi again became major while Ban Gu served as central protector.
translations.idiomatic: When Dou rose to Grand General, Fu Yi returned as army major while Ban Gu guarded headquarters.

sentences.zh: 宪府文章之盛，冠于当世。

translations.literal: The Dou mansion's literary brilliance capped the age.
translations.idiomatic: Dou's headquarters boasted the age's finest prose.

sentences.zh: 毅早卒，著诗、赋、诔、颂、祝文、《七激》、连珠凡二十八篇。

translations.literal: Yi died young; he left poems, fu, dirges, hymns, invocations, 《Seven Exhortations》, linked pearls—twenty-eight pieces.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi died young, leaving verse, fu, laments, songs, prayers, 《Seven Exhortations》, and linked pearls—twenty-eight works.

sentences.zh: 黄香字文强，江夏安陆人也。

translations.literal: Huang Xiang, courtesy name Wenqiang, was a native of Anlu in Jiangxia.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang, called Wenqiang, came from Anlu in Jiangxia.

sentences.zh: 年九岁，失母，思慕憔悴，殆不免丧，乡人称其至孝。

translations.literal: At nine he lost his mother; longing wasted him until he barely survived mourning; villagers called him supremely filial.
translations.idiomatic: He lost his mother at nine; grief wasted him until mourners feared he would follow her; neighbors praised his utmost filial devotion.

sentences.zh: 年十二，大守刘护闻而召之，署门下孝子，甚见爱敬。

translations.literal: At age twelve Grand Administrator Liu Hu heard of him and summoned him, appointing him Filial Son under his gate; he was greatly loved and respected.
translations.idiomatic: When he was twelve, Administrator Liu Hu summoned him and named him filial attendant at his residence—everyone cherished him.

sentences.zh: 香家贫，内无仆妾，躬执苦勤，尽心奉养。

translations.literal: The Huang household was poor and kept no servants or concubines; he personally endured bitter labor and devoted himself to supporting his parent.
translations.idiomatic: His family was destitute, without maids; he shouldered every hardship himself and nursed his father with utter devotion.

sentences.zh: 遂博学经典，究精道术，能文章，京师号曰“天下无双江夏黄童”。

translations.literal: Thereupon he became broadly learned in the classics, mastered techniques of the Way, and could compose; the capital dubbed him "the matchless lad of Jiangxia, Huang."
translations.idiomatic: He went on to master the canon and Daoist arts and to write brilliantly; the capital nicknamed him "the unrivaled Huang boy of Jiangxia."

sentences.zh: 初除郎中，元和元年，肃宗诏香诣东观，读所未尝见书。

translations.literal: First appointed gentleman; in the first Yuanhe year Emperor Zhang ordered Huang Xiang to the Eastern Lodge to read books he had never seen.
translations.idiomatic: His first post was gentleman; in Yuanhe 1 Emperor Zhang sent him to the Eastern Pavilion to devour texts he had never opened.

sentences.zh: 香后告休，及归京师，时千乘王冠，帝会中山邸，乃诏香殿下，顾谓诸王曰：“此‘天下无双江夏黄童’者也。

translations.literal: Later he requested leave and returned to the capital; when the Prince of Qiansheng received his cap, the emperor met the princes at the Zhongshan lodge and summoned Huang Xiang below the hall, saying to the kings: "This is the man called 'the matchless lad of Jiangxia, Huang.'"
translations.idiomatic: After he took leave and came back to Luoyang, the heir of Qiansheng was capped; at the Zhongshan hostel the emperor gathered the princes, called Huang Xiang forward, and told them: "Here is your 'matchless Huang lad of Jiangxia.'"

translations.literal: Those about him all changed how they regarded him.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone nearby revised his opinion at once.

sentences.zh: 后召诣安福殿言政事，拜尚书郎，数陈得失，赏赉增加。

translations.literal: Later he was summoned to Anfu Hall to discuss policy; appointed Gentleman of the Masters of Writing; repeatedly laid out gains and losses; rewards grew.
translations.idiomatic: He was next called to Anfu Hall for statecraft debates, made a Masters of Writing gentleman, spoke bluntly on policy, and watched stipends swell.

sentences.zh: 常独止宿台上，昼夜不离省闼，帝闻善之。

translations.literal: He often lodged alone on the terrace offices, day and night without leaving the palace compound; the emperor approved.
translations.idiomatic: He slept on duty in the terrace offices and barely stepped outside the palace gates; the throne praised such zeal.

translations.literal: Fourth Yongyuan year: appointed Left Assistant.
translations.idiomatic: In Yongyuan 4 he became Left Assistant.

translations.literal: His merit complete, he merited promotion; Emperor He kept him and raised his salary grade.
translations.idiomatic: His tour qualified him for advancement, yet Emperor He held him back with a higher stipend.

translations.literal: Sixth year: cumulatively promoted to Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: By year six he had climbed to Prefect of the Masters of Writing.

sentences.zh: 后以为东郡太守，香上疏让曰：“臣江淮孤贱，愚□小生，经学行能，无可算录。

translations.literal: Later appointed Administrator of Dong commandery; Huang Xiang submitted a memorial declining: "Your servant is base-born between the Yangzi and Huai, a foolish young student—the graph for one word is missing—without measurable achievement in classical learning or conduct."
translations.idiomatic: Named Dong commandery administrator, he memorialized to refuse: "I am a nobody from the Yangzi-Huai region, a raw student—one character is damaged in the text—with no record of learning or conduct worth citing."

sentences.zh: 遭值太平，先人余福，得以弱冠特蒙征用，连阶累任，遂极台阁。

translations.literal: Encountering an age of Great Peace and relying on ancestors’ leftover fortune, in weak-cap years he alone received special summons; rank followed rank until he reached the summit of the Terrace offices.
translations.idiomatic: Living under universal peace on inherited luck, he was plucked while still young, climbed step after step, and ended atop the Masters of Writing.

sentences.zh: 讫无纤介称，报恩效死，诚不意悟。

translations.literal: Never had I the slightest merit to record; to repay grace with my life would still fall short—I truly did not expect such favor.
translations.idiomatic: I had not a hair’s breadth of achievement; dying for the throne would barely repay it—I never dreamed of such grace.

sentences.zh: 卒被非望，显拜近郡，尊位千里。

translations.literal: Suddenly heaped with undeserved honor, plainly appointed to a nearby commandery of thousand-li dignity.
translations.idiomatic: Now I am thrust into honors I never sought—openly named to a neighboring province ruling a thousand li.

sentences.zh: 臣闻量能授官，则职无废事；

translations.literal: Your servant has heard that matching capacity when granting office leaves no duty undone;
translations.idiomatic: They say grant office to fit the man and no portfolio sits idle;

translations.literal: granting ranks according to labor keeps worthy and simple in proper balance.
translations.idiomatic: award fiefs for real labor and wise and plain men each find their place.

sentences.zh: 臣香小丑，少为诸生，典郡从政，固非所堪。

translations.literal: Your servant Xiang is a petty man, formerly only a student; to administer a commandery and govern is truly beyond what I can bear.
translations.idiomatic: I am a nobody who once merely studied; commanding a commandery is beyond my strength.

translations.literal: I truly fear ruin—one graph missing in the text—and alone shame the holy grace.
translations.idiomatic: I dread collapse—the manuscript leaves a gap—and would stain heaven’s favor.

sentences.zh: 又惟机密端首，至为尊要，复非臣香所当久奉。

translations.literal: Moreover the pivot of state secrets is supremely exalted and crucial—not something your servant Xiang should long hold.
translations.idiomatic: The nerve center of policy is too august for me to clutch forever.

translations.literal: Receiving the edict I tremble in panic and know not how to decide.
translations.idiomatic: The summons leaves me shaking; I cannot choose what to do.

sentences.zh: 臣香年在方刚，适可驱使。

translations.literal: Your servant Xiang’s years stand in their prime—just fit to be driven on errands.
translations.idiomatic: I am still in vigorous mid-life—fit only to run errands.

sentences.zh: 愿乞余恩，留备冗官，赐以督责小职，任之宫台烦事，以毕臣香蝼蚁小志，诚瞑目至愿，土灰极荣。

translations.literal: I beg leftover grace: retain me as a supernumerary, assign me a petty supervisory chore, burden me with vexing terrace paperwork so I may fulfill my ant-like ambition—closing my eyes in peace would be my utmost wish; dust and ash would crown my glory.
translations.idiomatic: Let me stay a spare hand, give me some nagging clerk’s duty, pile on palace busywork—that would satisfy my insect-small ambition; I could die content; ash on my name would feel like glory.

sentences.zh: ”帝亦惜香干用，久习旧事，复留为尚书令，增秩二千石，赐钱三十万。

translations.literal: The emperor also prized Xiang’s capability and long familiarity with precedent; again retained him as Prefect of the Masters of Writing, raised his salary to two thousand shi, and granted three hundred thousand cash.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor valued his competence and intimate knowledge of routine, kept him as Prefect of the Masters of Writing, bumped his rank to two thousand shi, and handed him three hundred thousand cash.

sentences.zh: 是后遂管枢机，甚见亲重，而香亦□勤物务，忧公如家。

translations.literal: After this he managed the pivot of power and was greatly trusted; Huang Xiang also—the graph is damaged—diligently handled affairs and worried for the public like his own household.
translations.idiomatic: From then on he steered the machinery of state and won deep trust; Huang Xiang too—one character missing—threw himself into paperwork and treated the realm like kin.

sentences.zh: 十二年，东平清河奏訞言卿仲辽等，所连及且千人。

translations.literal: Twelfth year: Dongping and Qinghe submitted accusations concerning Qing Zhongliao and others; those implicated approached a thousand.
translations.idiomatic: In year twelve Dongping and Qinghe reported charges linking Qing Zhongliao and others until nearly a thousand names tangled in the net.

translations.literal: Xiang separately weighed the evidence in each memorial and spared very many lives.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang parsed each dossier and kept countless people alive.

sentences.zh: 每郡国疑罪，辄务求轻科，爱惜人命，每存忧济。

translations.literal: Whenever commanderies forwarded doubtful crimes he always sought the lightest statute, cherishing human life and preserving compassionate relief.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever a province sent up ambiguous cases he leaned toward lenient clauses, guarding lives and easing distress.

sentences.zh: 又晓习边事，均量军政，皆得事宜。

translations.literal: He also understood frontier affairs and balanced military administration—all matched what was fitting.
translations.idiomatic: He knew border affairs and weighed army logistics so decisions always fit circumstances.

translations.literal: The emperor knew his meticulous diligence and repeatedly added rewards.
translations.idiomatic: The throne saw his grind and showered extra gifts.

translations.literal: When ill he received imperial inquiries and medicine.
translations.idiomatic: Sickness brought court messengers and imperial physic.

sentences.zh: 在位多所荐达，宠遇甚盛，议者讥其过幸。

translations.literal: In office he recommended many men for advancement; favor was extreme; critics mocked his excessive fortune.
translations.idiomatic: He promoted throngs of talent and soaked up favor until gossip called him over-lucky.

translations.literal: First Yanping year: transferred to Administrator of Wei commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Yanping 1 moved him to Wei commandery administrator.

sentences.zh: 郡旧有内外园田，常与人分种，收谷岁数千斛。

translations.literal: The commandery formerly held inner and outer garden plots; they regularly shared planting with others and collected several thousand hu of grain yearly.
translations.idiomatic: The prefecture once leased palace gardens inside and out, sharecropping them for thousands of hu a year.

sentences.zh: 香曰：“《田令》‘商者不农’，《王制》‘仕者不耕’，伐冰食禄之人，不与百姓争利。

translations.literal: Xiang said: 《Field Ordinance》 states "merchants do not farm"; 《Royal Regulations》 states "officeholders do not plough"; men who harvest ice and eat stipends must not vie with commoners for profit.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang cited 《Field Ordinance》: merchants do not till; 《Royal Regulations》: officers do not hold the plough—salary men must not squeeze the people.

translations.literal: Thereupon he entirely assigned the plots to commoners and assessed them for cultivation.
translations.idiomatic: He handed every plot to the people and taxed the harvest fairly.

sentences.zh: 时被水年肌，乃分奉禄及所得赏赐班赡贫者，于是丰富之家各出义谷，助官禀贷，荒民获全。

translations.literal: When flood seasons brought famine he divided his salary and grants to relieve the poor; wealthy households then contributed righteous grain to supplement official granaries, and starving people survived.
translations.idiomatic: When floods brought lean years he split stipends and gifts to feed the needy; rich families poured charity grain into state relief and refugees lived.

sentences.zh: 后坐水潦事免，数月，卒于家。

translations.literal: Later dismissed over flood litigation; several months later died at home.
translations.idiomatic: Flood paperwork cost him his post; months later he died at home.

sentences.zh: 所著贼、笺、奏、书、令、凡五篇。

translations.literal: His writings—fu, notes, memorials, letters, directives—five pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: He left five pieces: fu, memoranda, memorials, letters, and orders.

translations.literal: His son Qiong has his own biography.
translations.idiomatic: His son Huang Qiong receives a separate biography.

translations.literal: Liu Yi was a son of Prince Jing of Beihai.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yi belonged to Prince Jing of Beihai’s house.

sentences.zh: 初封平望侯，永元中，坐事夺爵。

translations.literal: First enfeoffed Marquis of Pingwang; in Yongyuan stripped of the fief for an offense.
translations.idiomatic: He began as Marquis of Pingwang but Yongyuan stripped him for a crime.

translations.literal: Yi from youth was famed for literary eloquence.
translations.idiomatic: Even young he was known for rhetorical skill.

sentences.zh: 元初元年，上《汉德论》并《宪论》十二篇。

translations.literal: First Yuanchu year he presented 《Discourse on Han Virtue》 and 《Discourse on the Charter》—twelve chapters.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanchu 1 saw him submit twelve chapters titled 《Discourse on Han Virtue》 and 《Discourse on the Charter》.

sentences.zh: 时，刘珍、邓耽、尹兑、马融共上书称其美，安帝嘉之，赐钱三万，拜议郎。

translations.literal: At the time Liu Zhen, Deng Dan, Yin Dui, and Ma Rong jointly memorialized praising him; Emperor An commended him, granted thirty thousand cash, and appointed Counselor.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Zhen, Deng Dan, Yin Dui, and Ma Rong praised him in a joint memorial; Emperor An gave thirty thousand cash and made him a counselor.

sentences.zh: 李尤字伯仁，广汉雒人也。

translations.literal: Li You, courtesy name Boren, was a native of Luo in Guanghan.
translations.idiomatic: Li You, called Boren, came from Luo in Guanghan.

translations.literal: In youth he rose to fame through writing.
translations.idiomatic: He won notice young on the strength of his prose.

sentences.zh: 和帝时，侍中贾逵荐尤有相如、杨雄之风，召诣东观，受诏作赋，拜兰台令史。

translations.literal: Under Emperor He, Palace Attendant Jia Kui recommended You as having the manner of Xiangru and Yang Xiong; summoned to the Eastern Lodge, ordered to compose fu, appointed Orchid Terrace clerk.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor He’s attendant Jia Kui likened him to Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong; summoned to the Eastern Lodge for commissioned fu, he became Orchid Terrace clerk.

sentences.zh: 稍迁，安帝时为谏议大夫，受诏与谒者仆射刘珍等俱撰《汉记》。

translations.literal: Gradually promoted; under Emperor An he was remonstrance counselor; ordered with Herald Superintendent Liu Zhen and others to compile 《Han Records》.
translations.idiomatic: Promoted stepwise, he served Emperor An as remonstrance counselor and joined Herald chief Liu Zhen to compile 《Han Records》.

sentences.zh: 后帝废太子为济阴王，尤上书谏争。

translations.literal: Later the emperor demoted the heir apparent to Prince of Jiyin; You submitted a memorial remonstrating.
translations.idiomatic: When the heir was demoted to prince of Jiyin, Li You protested in writing.

translations.literal: When Emperor Shun ascended, promoted to Chancellor of Le’an.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shun raised him to Le’an chancellor.

translations.literal: Died at eighty-three.
translations.idiomatic: He died at eighty-three.

sentences.zh: 所著诗、赋、铭、诔、颂、《七叹》、《哀典》，凡二十八篇。

translations.literal: His writings: poems, fu, inscriptions, dirges, hymns, 《Seven Laments》, 《Canon of Lament》—twenty-eight pieces.
translations.idiomatic: He left twenty-eight works: verse, fu, inscriptions, laments, songs, 《Seven Laments》, and 《Canon of Lament》.

sentences.zh: 尤同郡李胜，亦有文才，为东观郎，著赋、诔、颂、论数十篇。

translations.literal: Li Sheng of the same commandery also had literary talent; served as Eastern Lodge gentleman; composed several tens of fu, dirges, hymns, and treatises.
translations.idiomatic: His townsman Li Sheng wrote well too, served as an Eastern Lodge gentleman, and left dozens of fu, laments, hymns, and essays.

sentences.zh: 苏顺字孝山，京兆霸陵人也。

translations.literal: Su Shun, courtesy name Xiaoshan, was a native of Baling in Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Su Shun, styled Xiaoshan, hailed from Baling in Jingzhao.

translations.literal: Between the He and An reigns he was renowned for talent and learning.
translations.idiomatic: Between Emperors He and An he was celebrated for scholarship.

translations.literal: He loved techniques of nurturing life and lived in reclusion seeking the Way.
translations.idiomatic: He pursued longevity arts and hid in the hills to cultivate Dao.

translations.literal: Only late did he take office; appointed gentleman; died in office.
translations.idiomatic: He entered service late as a gentleman and died on duty.

sentences.zh: 所著贼、论、诔、哀辞、杂文，凡十六篇。

translations.literal: His writings: fu, treatises, dirges, elegies, miscellaneous pieces—sixteen in all.
translations.idiomatic: Sixteen pieces survive: fu, essays, laments, dirges, and miscellany.

sentences.zh: 时，三辅多士，扶风曹众伯师亦有才学，著诔、书、论四篇。

translations.literal: At the time the Three Adjuncts teemed with scholars; Cao Zhong of Fufeng, style Boshi, also had talent and learning; composed four pieces of dirges, letters, and treatises.
translations.idiomatic: The capital surrounds brimmed with talent—Cao Zhong of Fufeng, called Boshi, wrote four laments, letters, and treatises.

sentences.zh: 又有曹朔，不知何许人，作《汉颂》四篇。

translations.literal: There was also Cao Shuo of unknown origin who composed four chapters of 《Han Eulogy》.
translations.idiomatic: Another Cao Shuo, birthplace unknown, penned four chapters of 《Han Eulogy》.

sentences.zh: 葛龚字元甫，梁国宁陵人也。

translations.literal: Ge Gong, courtesy name Yuanfu, was a native of Ningling in Liang.
translations.idiomatic: Ge Gong, styled Yuanfu, came from Ningling in Liang.

translations.literal: Under Emperor He he was known for skill in documentary writing.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor He knew him for crisp paperwork.

translations.literal: His nature was forthright and fierce; courage and strength surpassed others.
translations.idiomatic: He was bold and blunt, stronger than most.

sentences.zh: 安帝永初中，举孝廉，为太官丞，上便宜四事，拜荡阴令。

translations.literal: In Yongchu of Emperor An, recommended filial and incorrupt; served as Privy Treasurer aide; submitted four convenient proposals; appointed magistrate of Tangyin.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor An’s Yongchu term brought a filial-incorrupt nomination, a stint as imperial kitchen aide, four policy memos, and the Tangyin magistracy.

translations.literal: Summoned to the Grand Commandant’s office—illness prevented him from taking the post.
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Commandant called him in, but illness blocked the appointment.

translations.literal: The province recommended abundant talent; appointed magistrate of Linfen.
translations.idiomatic: Provincial abundant-talent nomination landed him the Linfen magistracy.

translations.literal: In both counties he left praiseworthy administrative records.
translations.idiomatic: Both postings earned glowing reviews.

sentences.zh: 著文、贼、碑、诔、书记，凡十二篇。

translations.literal: He composed prose, fu, stele texts, dirges, letters—twelve pieces.
translations.idiomatic: Twelve works remain: essays, fu, stele inscriptions, laments, correspondence.

sentences.zh: 王逸字叔师，南郡宜城人也。

translations.literal: Wang Yi, courtesy name Shushi, was a native of Yicheng in Nan commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Yi, called Shushi, was from Yicheng in Nan commandery.

sentences.zh: 元初中，举上计吏，为校书郎。

translations.literal: In early Yuanchu recommended as chief clerk for accounts; became collator.
translations.idiomatic: Early Yuanchu brought him up as chief clerk for the accounts survey, then collator.

translations.literal: Under Emperor Shun he was palace attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shun named him palace attendant.

translations.literal: He authored 《Chu Lyrics with Commentary》, which circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: His 《Chu Lyrics with Commentary》 circulated widely.

sentences.zh: 其赋、诔、书、论及杂文，凡二十一篇。

translations.literal: His fu, dirges, letters, treatises, and miscellaneous writings—twenty-one pieces.
translations.idiomatic: Twenty-one pieces survive: fu, laments, letters, essays, and scraps.

translations.literal: He also composed 《Han Verses》—123 chapters.
translations.idiomatic: He added 123 chapters titled 《Han Verses》.

translations.literal: His son Yanshou, courtesy name Wenkao, had outstanding talent.
translations.idiomatic: His son Wang Yanshou, styled Wenkao, burned bright.

translations.literal: In youth he traveled to Lu and composed 《Hall of Spiritual Light Fu》.
translations.idiomatic: Young, he studied in Lu and wrote 《Hall of Spiritual Light Fu》.

sentences.zh: 后蔡邕亦造此赋，未成，及见延寿所为，甚奇之，遂辍翰而已。

translations.literal: Later Cai Yong also undertook this fu but did not finish; when he saw what Yanshou had done he marveled greatly and laid down his brush.
translations.idiomatic: Cai Yong later tried the same theme, saw Yanshou’s draft, marveled, and quit.

sentences.zh: 曾有异梦，意恶之，乃作《梦赋》以自厉。

translations.literal: Once he had an ominous dream; loathing it he composed 《Dream Fu》 to brace himself.
translations.idiomatic: A nightmare spurred him to compose 《Dream Fu》 as self-warning.

translations.literal: Later he drowned; aged a little over twenty.
translations.idiomatic: He drowned before thirty.

sentences.zh: 崔琦字子玮，涿郡安平人，济北相瑗之宗也。

translations.literal: Cui Qi, courtesy name Ziwei, was a man of Anping in Zhuo commandery, of the same lineage as Chancellor of Jinbei Cui Yuan.
translations.idiomatic: Cui Qi, styled Ziwei, from Anping in Zhuo, shared descent with Jinbei chancellor Cui Yuan.

sentences.zh: 少游学京师，以文章博通称。

translations.literal: In youth he studied in the capital and was famed for broad literary mastery.
translations.idiomatic: He read in Luoyang and passed for omnivorously learned.

translations.literal: First recommended filial and incorrupt; appointed gentleman.
translations.idiomatic: Filial-incorrupt nomination made him a gentleman.

sentences.zh: 河南尹梁冀闻其才，请与交。

translations.literal: Governor of Henan Liang Ji heard of his talent and asked to associate with him.
translations.idiomatic: Henan governor Liang Ji courted his friendship.

sentences.zh: 冀行多不轨，琦数引古今成败以戒之，冀不能受。

translations.literal: Ji acted often beyond bounds; Qi repeatedly cited ancient and modern success and failure to warn him; Ji could not accept it.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji swaggered past law; Cui Qi warned him with historical parallels until Ji refused to listen.

translations.literal: Thereupon he composed 《Admonition for In-laws》.
translations.idiomatic: So he wrote 《Admonition for In-laws》.

translations.literal: Its words say.
translations.idiomatic: It opens.

translations.literal: Illustrious, illustrious the imperial in-laws—splendor blazing bright.
translations.idiomatic: Splendid are the imperial in-laws—glory dazzling the court.

translations.literal: Anciently under Emperor Shun virtue rose through Ying and Huang.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shun’s virtue shone through his Ying and Huang consorts.

translations.literal: Zhou rose through three mothers; Youxin honored Tang.
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou house leaned on three royal mothers; Youxin ladies lifted Tang.

translations.literal: King Xuan of Zhou slept late; Jiang the queen removed her hairpins.
translations.idiomatic: King Xuan of Zhou lingered in bed until Queen Jiang pulled her pins.

translations.literal: Duke Huan of Qi loved music; Lady Wei of Wei gave no tunes.
translations.idiomatic: Duke Huan of Qi craved song—Lady Wei of Wei withheld her zither.

sentences.zh: 皆辅主以礼，扶君以仁，达才进善，以义济身。

translations.literal: All aided their lords by ritual, supported them by benevolence, advanced talent and goodness, and aided themselves by righteousness.
translations.idiomatic: Each aided her lord with ritual, steadied him with kindness, lifted worthy men, and walked by righteousness.

translations.literal: Down to late generations decline gradually crumbled.
translations.idiomatic: Later ages slid toward ruin.

translations.literal: Fish strung on a cord lost order; the nine concubines fell into confusion.
translations.idiomatic: The queenly order unraveled like slanting fish on a string; the nine inner ranks stumbled.

translations.literal: Jin state’s calamity—disaster arose from Li Ji.
translations.idiomatic: Jin’s doom began with Lady Li Ji.

translations.literal: 'Ruin to the household.'
translations.idiomatic: 'The house is undone.'

translations.literal: 'The hen's morning crow.'
translations.idiomatic: 'The hen crows dawn.'

translations.literal: Monopolizing power and favor, displaying oneself while blocking others.
translations.idiomatic: They hoard favor, flaunt themselves, and shut others out.

translations.literal: Bullying elders and estranging old ties, destroying and stripping the nearest kin.
translations.idiomatic: They browbeat elders, cut old bonds, and tear even flesh and blood.

translations.literal: Co-equal queens rivaled legitimate heirs; licentious women destroyed Chen.
translations.idiomatic: Shared standing with the heir and rival consorts brought Chen to ruin through wanton women.

translations.literal: The unworthy were raised aloft; Fan became Minister of Education.
translations.idiomatic: Mediocre men gained the summit—Fan rose to Minister of Education.

translations.literal: They bore noble titles yet rode beyond their station; they harvested stipends from famed capitals.
translations.idiomatic: They wore rank like porters on fine horses and drew rents from great cities.

translations.literal: The poets therefore satirize them; virtue applied brings no lasting ease.
translations.idiomatic: The Odes skewer such houses—virtue practiced yields no careless peace.

translations.literal: Cruel Xin was beguiled by a woman; rejecting counsel he isolated himself.
translations.idiomatic: King Zhou of Shang drowned in a woman's flattery and deafened himself to every warning.

translations.literal: Bat-winged and serpent-hearted, he poured poison on the guiltless.
