translations.idiomatic: His heart was bat-foul and viper-vicious; he poured cruelty on the innocent.

translations.literal: He slew his uncles and carved open pregnant women.
translations.idiomatic: He murdered fathers and brothers and ripped open women big with child.

translations.literal: Heaven roared anger and earth swelled with wrath; men plotted and ghosts designed his fall.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven and earth burned with rage; living men and angry spirits closed the net.

translations.literal: On the jiazi dawn body and head were parted.
translations.idiomatic: At gray dawn on the day jiazi his trunk and skull went separate ways.

translations.literal: First he was Son of Heaven; afterward he became another man's hornless dragon.
translations.idiomatic: Yesterday Son of Heaven; today plaything under another's claw.

translations.literal: It was not lust alone—the mothers of empresses did worse.
translations.idiomatic: The vice reached beyond rouged chambers—dowager intrigues matched them.

sentences.zh: 不相率以礼，而竞奖以权。

translations.literal: They did not guide one another by ritual but raced to prize naked power.
translations.idiomatic: They spurned ritual leadership for the naked scramble after leverage.

translations.literal: They laughed first and wailed after—ending in shame and mutilation.
translations.idiomatic: They began in laughter and ended in howls—ruin and maiming were the close.

translations.literal: The nation vanished; ancestral temples went up in flame.
translations.idiomatic: The dynasty guttered out; ancestral halls turned to ash.

sentences.zh: 末嬉丧夏，褒姒毙周，妲已亡殷，赵灵沙丘。

translations.literal: Mojie ended Xia; Baosi broke Zhou; Daji sank Yin; King Ling of Zhao died at Shaqiu.
translations.idiomatic: Mojie drowned Xia, Baosi broke Zhou, Daji sank Yin, and King Ling of Zhao wasted away at Shaqiu.

translations.literal: Lady Qi became a human pig; the Lu clan collapsed.
translations.idiomatic: Concubine Qi was carved into a human pig; the Lu house crashed.

translations.literal: Empress Chen practiced witchcraft and at last died beyond the palace.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Chen's sorcery earned exile and a lonely death.

translations.literal: Huo meant to poison the heir-apparent and herself fell stripped of rank.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Huo plotted poison for the crown prince and lost her own throne.

sentences.zh: 故曰：无谓我贵，天将尔摧；

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: 'Do not boast that you are noble—Heaven will tear you down.'
translations.idiomatic: So the maxim runs: cry 'noble' all you like—Heaven still pulls you down.

translations.literal: 'Do not trust lasting beauty—radiance always fades.'
translations.idiomatic: Never bank on a pretty face—the bloom always thins.

translations.literal: 'Do not cling to constant favor—love always slackens.'
translations.idiomatic: Never cling to favor—it always ebbs.

translations.literal: 'Do not cry that you alone are strong—Heaven and men turn against you.'
translations.idiomatic: Boast 'I am able' and Heaven and the crowd wheel against you.

translations.literal: Calamity sprouts where virtue fails; fortune hinges on cautious pivot.
translations.idiomatic: Disaster grows from moral slack; luck hangs on a careful hinge.

translations.literal: The sun does not linger at noon; the full moon must wane.
translations.idiomatic: The sun never parks at zenith; the swollen moon must hollow.

translations.literal: Those who walk the Way stand firm; those who lean on power totter.
translations.idiomatic: Tread the Dao and you root deep; ride brute force and you tip.

translations.literal: Your petty servant oversees imperial affines—here I dare proclaim it.
translations.idiomatic: I, least among ministers charged with kinsmen—here is my warning.

sentences.zh: 琦以言不从，失意，复作《白鹄赋》以为风。

translations.literal: Because his advice went unheeded Qi grew despondent and composed 《White Swan Fu》 as indirect criticism.
translations.idiomatic: Ignored by Liang Ji, Cui Qi wrote 《White Swan Fu》 to needle him obliquely.

sentences.zh: 梁冀见之，呼琦问曰：“百官外内，各有司存，天下云云，岂独吾人之尤，君何激刺之过乎！

translations.literal: Liang Ji read it and summoned Qi, demanding: 'Court and capital each has its duties; murmurs fill the realm—is my house alone to blame? Why stab so viciously at me!'
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji called him in: everyone has an office; gossip runs everywhere—why blame only us? Why cut so deep with satire!

sentences.zh: ”琦对曰：“昔管仲相齐，乐闻机谏之言；

translations.literal: Qi replied: 'Anciently Guan Zhong served Qi and loved to hear subtle remonstrance.'
translations.idiomatic: Cui Qi answered: Guan Zhong serving Qi thirsted for delicate warnings.

sentences.zh: 萧何佐汉，乃设书过之吏。

translations.literal: 'Xiao He aided Han and even posted clerks to record faults.'
translations.idiomatic: Xiao He serving Han assigned clerks to write down missteps.

sentences.zh: 今将军累世台辅，任齐伊、公，而德政未闻，黎元涂炭。

translations.literal: 'Today you, general, have filled generation after generation as pillar minister—your burden rivals Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou—yet worthy rule is unheard and the common folk lie charred in ruin.'
translations.idiomatic: You have been the dynasty's backbone for generations—weight like Yi Yin or the Duke of Zhou—yet no humane rule appears and the people burn in misery.

sentences.zh: 不能结纳贞良，以救祸败，反复欲钳塞士口，杜蔽主听，将使玄黄改色，马鹿易形乎？

translations.literal: 'Unable to gather upright men to stem disaster, you would gag scholars and deafen the sovereign—do you mean to swap black for yellow and turn horses into deer?'
translations.idiomatic: You neither recruit good men to stop collapse nor open your ears—you would gag every tongue until truth inverts like swapping horse for deer?

translations.literal: Ji could not answer and sent Qi away.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji had nothing to say and dismissed him.

sentences.zh: 后除为临济长，不敢之职，解印绶去。

translations.literal: Later appointed magistrate of Linji, he dared not take office and surrendered his seal.
translations.idiomatic: Named magistrate of Linji, he refused the post and laid down his ribbons.

translations.literal: Ji thereupon ordered assassins to hunt him down.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji then sent killers after him.

sentences.zh: 客见琦耕于陌上，怀书一卷，息辄偃而咏之。

translations.literal: An assassin saw Qi plowing a path-edge furrow, a scroll tucked in his bosom; whenever he rested he reclined and chanted.
translations.idiomatic: A killer found him behind the plow with a book at his breast, chanting each time he rested.

sentences.zh: 客哀其志，以实告琦，曰：“将军令吾要子，今见君贤者，情怀忍忍。

translations.literal: The man pitied his resolve and confessed: 'The general ordered me to stop you; seeing your virtue my heart cannot bear it.'
translations.idiomatic: The assassin pitied him and admitted the contract—yet honor stayed his hand.

sentences.zh: 可亟自逃，吾亦于此亡矣。

translations.literal: 'Flee now—I too disappear from here.'
translations.idiomatic: Flee at once—I vanish as well.

translations.literal: Qi escaped; Ji later seized and executed him.
translations.idiomatic: Cui Qi fled, but Liang Ji caught him in the end and put him to death.

sentences.zh: 所著赋、颂、铭、诔、箴、吊、论、《九咨》、《七言》，凡十五篇。

translations.literal: His writings include fu, hymns, inscriptions, dirges, admonitions, condolences, treatises, 《Nine Consultations》, and 《Seven-Character Lines》—fifteen pieces.
translations.idiomatic: He left fifteen works: fu, songs, stele texts, laments, warnings, elegies, essays, 《Nine Consultations》, and 《Seven-Character Lines》.

sentences.zh: 边韶字孝先，陈留浚仪人也。

translations.literal: Bian Shao, courtesy name Xiaoxian, was a native of Junyi in Chenliu.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Shao, styled Xiaoxian, came from Junyi in Chenliu.

sentences.zh: 以文章知名，教授数百人。

translations.literal: He was famed for letters and taught several hundred disciples.
translations.idiomatic: His prose won renown and his lecture hall held hundreds.

sentences.zh: 韶口辩，曾昼日假卧，弟子私嘲之曰：“边孝先，腹便便。

translations.literal: Shao was eloquent; once he napped by day and students mocked him in secret: 'Bian Xiaoxian—big belly round.'
translations.idiomatic: Quick with words, he once dozed in daylight; pupils whispered: 'Bian Xiaoxian's belly sticks way out.'

translations.literal: 'Lazy with books—only wants sleep.'
translations.idiomatic: 'Too lazy to read—only wants to sleep.'

sentences.zh: ”韶潜闻之，应时对曰：“边为姓、考为字。

translations.literal: Shao overheard and shot back: 'Bian is the surname, Xiao the style.'
translations.idiomatic: Bian Shao heard and answered: 'Bian names the clan, Xiao the style.'

translations.literal: 'The big belly—stores for 《Five Classics》.'
translations.idiomatic: 'That belly—it's a granary for 《Five Classics》.'

translations.literal: 'Sleep alone—pondering the classics.'
translations.idiomatic: 'Wanting sleep—chewing on the canon.'

sentences.zh: 寐与周公通梦，静与孔子同意。

translations.literal: 'In dreams I traffic with the Duke of Zhou; in stillness I agree with Confucius.'
translations.idiomatic: 'Asleep I bargain with the Duke of Zhou; awake in silence I match Confucius.'

translations.literal: 'Mock your teacher—what canonical warrant allows it?'
translations.idiomatic: 'If masters may be mocked, what classic permits it?'

translations.literal: The mockers burned with shame.
translations.idiomatic: The hecklers shrank away ashamed.

translations.literal: Shao's wit was ever thus.
translations.idiomatic: His repartee always landed like this.

sentences.zh: 桓帝时，为临颍侯相，征拜太中大夫，著作东观。

translations.literal: Under Emperor Huan he served as chancellor to the marquis of Linying, was summoned Grand Palace Grandee, and composed at the Eastern Lodge.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Huan made him tutor to the marquis of Linying, then Grand Palace Grandee composing at the Eastern Lodge.

sentences.zh: 再迁北地太守，入拜尚书令。

translations.literal: Promoted again to Administrator of Beidi, then entered court as Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to Beidi administrator and later Prefect of the Masters of Writing.

translations.literal: Later Chancellor of Chen—he died in office.
translations.idiomatic: His last post was Chen chancellor; he died on duty.

sentences.zh: 著诗、颂、碑、铭、书、策，凡十五篇。

translations.literal: He composed poems, hymns, stele texts, inscriptions, letters, and policy memorials—fifteen pieces.
translations.idiomatic: Fifteen pieces remain: verse, songs, stele inscriptions, essays, letters, and memorials.
